parts.problem_md:
A shopkeeper sells fruit and has created a table containing the name of the fruit, its bar code number and an image of the bar code.

**State **and describe **two **validation checks that could be used for the bar code number.
parts.solution_md:
Examples of validation checks that could be used include:

Any matching validation check & description:

- **Check digit** – An extra digit added to a number which is calculated from the other digits, this ensures the rest of the number is correct **[1 mark]**
- **Length check** – Checks that there are only 12 characters **[1 mark]**
- **Presence check** – Checks that the number exists in the table / not a null value **[1 mark]**
- **Type check** – Checks that the data entered is an integer **[1 mark]**
- **Character check** – Checks that the data entered are only numbers **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md: **Describe **the benefits and drawbacks of using parallel running.
parts.solution_md:
Examples of the benefits of using parallel running include:

Max **four **of the following:

- If the new system fails the old one is still available for a time to be used **[1 mark]**
- Less data will be lost during implementation **[1 mark]**
- Training is gradual **[1 mark]**
- New system can be easily tested with live data **[1 mark]**

Examples of the drawbacks of using parallel running include:

Max **four **of the following:

- Implementation is expensive as two sets of staff are needed **[1 mark]**
- Two systems are needed therefore more expensive **[1 mark]**
- There will be duplication of data entry which can cause differences in the output of the two systems **[1 mark]**
- More time consuming to enter data into two systems **[1 mark]**
- Two systems take up more physical space **[1 mark]**

Any **two **of the following:

- Parallel running is running both systems together until the new system works properly/fully implemented **[1 mark]**
- When the new system works, the old system is removed **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
A company with many branches is implementing a new system. The manager is planning to implement the new system either by pilot changeover or parallel running.

**Compare **pilot changeover and parallel running.
parts.solution_md:
**Parallel running**

- Both systems operate together until the old one is removed **[1 mark]**
- Staff can be trained on the whole system gradually **[1 mark]**
- More time consuming to enter data into two systems **[1 mark]**
- If the new system fails then the old system is there for a while to be used **[1 mark]**
- It is more expensive as two sets of staff are needed **[1 mark] **
- It is more expensive as two systems are needed **[1 mark]**

**Pilot Changeover**

- Each branch is implemented separately **[1 mark]**
- Each <u>branch </u>changing over only uses the new system **[1 mark]**
- Costs are reduced as only one branch is affected at a time **[1 mark]**
- If there is an error in the new system only one branch is affected **[1 mark]**
- Staff can be trained in the branch being implemented **[1 mark]**
- The changeover is easier to manage **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
The owner of Tawara Hotels is planning a new computerised booking system. There are ten Tawara Hotels throughout the world. The current booking system allows people to book rooms in any of 7 the Tawara Hotels. He has employed a systems analyst to research the current system and then install the new system.

Before the new booking system is installed, the systems analyst has to decide on a method of implementation. One method of implementation is pilot running.

**Name** two other methods of implementation and **describe **two benefits of each.
parts.solution_md:
Two other methods of implementation include:

**One **mark for method, max **two **for benefit:

**Direct changeover** **[1 mark]**

- Benefits are immediate **[1 mark]**
- Costs less as fewer staff are needed **[1 mark]**
- Costs less as only one system is required **[1 mark]**
- Less likelihood of malfunction as system is fully tested **[1 mark]**

**Parallel running ****[1 mark]**

- If new system fails, old system can be used as a back up **[1 mark]**
- Possible to gradually train staff **[1 mark]**

**Phased changeover ****[1 mark]**

- If the new system fails, only one part is affected **[1 mark]**
- Easier to ensure that part of the system is fully operational before moving onto the next part **[1 mark]**
- Possible to train staff in one part of the system, therefore less costly than parallel **[1 mark]**
- Possible to gradually train staff **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
When a system is being planned, analysis needs to take place.

Questionnaires and interviews are examples of methods of researching existing systems.

**Evaluate**, by weighing up the advantages and disadvantages, each of these methods.
parts.solution_md:
Both questionnaires and interviews are useful methods for researching an existing system, but each has its advantages and disadvantages.

One advantage of questionnaires is that they are **quicker to complete**, allowing multiple people to respond at the same time. Additionally, questionnaires can be **completed in the respondent’s own time**, providing flexibility compared to interviews, which must be scheduled. Another key benefit is that responses can **remain anonymous**, making people more likely to give honest feedback.

However, questionnaires are** inflexible**, as they only allow for fixed responses, whereas interviews can be adjusted based on previous answers. Another drawback is that **respondents may not return questionnaires**, leading to a low response rate. Additionally, if a question is unclear, there is no way for the respondent to ask for clarification, which could result in misleading or inaccurate answers.

On the other hand, interviews allow for deeper discussions, as the interviewer can ask follow-up questions and adapt them based on previous responses. This makes them more flexible and allows for more detailed insights. However, interviews are **more expensive**, as businesses must pay for an interviewer and compensate employees for their time. Additionally, interviews are not anonymous, which may lead some respondents to withhold honest opinions.

Overall, questionnaires are more efficient for collecting large amounts of data, while interviews provide more detailed, flexible responses. The choice of method depends on the time, budget, and depth of information required.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Response includes at least three advantages and three disadvantages, ensuring a balanced evaluation.
> 
> - Questionnaires are quicker to complete **[1 mark]**
> - Questionnaires can be completed in the respondent’s own time **[1 mark]**
> - Questionnaires allow for anonymous responses **[1 mark]**
> - Questionnaires are inflexible, whereas interviews allow follow-up questions **[1 mark]**
> - Respondents may not return questionnaires **[1 mark]**
> - Interviews are more expensive due to staffing costs **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Five **top tips for answering this 6-mark "evaluate" question effectively:
> 
> 1. **Compare both methods equally**
> 
>   1. To get full marks, ensure you discuss three points for each method rather than focusing too much on one.
> 2. **Explain how interviews provide deeper insights**
> 
>   1. Example: Instead of just saying "interviews allow more detail," write "interviews allow follow-up questions, helping to explore answers in greater depth."
> 3. **Highlight why questionnaires are faster but less flexible**
> 
>   1. Mention that questionnaires allow responses from many people at once, but lack adaptability when answers need further explanation.
> 4. **Discuss time, cost, and accuracy factors**
> 
>   1. Example: "Interviews are expensive because the interviewer must be paid, whereas questionnaires can be distributed at a lower cost."
> 5. **Avoid vague statements**
> 
>   1. Instead of "people don’t always answer questionnaires," say "people may not return questionnaires, leading to a lower response rate."

parts.problem_md:
Different methods can be used to analyse a system.

**Discuss** the benefits and drawbacks of analysing a system by observing staff rather than looking at the current systems documentation.
parts.solution_md:
Analysing a system by observing staff instead of examining documents has several benefits. One advantage is that the **analyst sees the system in action**, allowing them to understand how staff interact with it in real time. Additionally, observation **provides a complete picture** of the system, including any inefficiencies that might not be recorded in documents. Another benefit is that it is less disruptive to workers, as they can continue their tasks while the analyst observes, **making it a cheaper method of analysis**.

However, observation also has drawbacks. The **quality and accuracy of the findings depend on the skill of the observer**, meaning mistakes or biases could affect the results. Another issue is the Hawthorne effect, where staff may change their behaviour when they know they are being watched, leading to inaccurate data.

On the other hand, examining existing documentation has advantages, such as **allowing the analyst to see exact details of inputs, processing, and outputs**, which can be more precise than observation. Additionally, previous system analysis reports may already exist, saving time in the research process. However, looking through documents is **time-consuming**, and hiring an analyst to examine records can be expensive.

Overall, while observation provides real-world insight into system usage, examining documents offers structured and precise information, though it requires more time and cost.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The response includes at least three advantages and three disadvantages, ensuring a balanced discussion.
> 
> - The analyst sees the system in action **[1 mark]**
> - Observation provides a complete picture **[1 mark]**
> - Cheaper as it does not take the worker away from work **[1 mark]**
> - The quality and accuracy of information is highly dependent on the skill of the observer **[1 mark]**
> - Examining documents shows exact details of inputs, processing, and outputs **[1 mark]**
> - Very time-consuming to look through all the documents **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Five **top tips for answering this 6-mark "discuss" question effectively:
> 
> 1. **Include at least three points for both observation and examining documents**
> 
>   1. A balanced response is necessary to get full marks.
> 2. **Explain why observation is useful but not always reliable**
> 
>   1. Example: Instead of just saying "observation provides a complete picture," write "observation helps analysts see real-world system usage, but staff may alter their behaviour due to the Hawthorne effect."
> 3. **Highlight why examining documents can be more precise**
> 
>   1. Mention that documents provide exact details about inputs, processing, and outputs, which may not be as clear from observation.
> 4. **Consider time and cost factors**
> 
>   1. Example: "Examining documents can be time-consuming and expensive, whereas observation is cheaper as it does not disrupt staff."
> 5. **Avoid vague points**
> 
>   1. Instead of "documents take a long time," explain "analysing large amounts of paperwork is slow and costly, as it requires hiring an experienced analyst."

parts.problem_md:
A system can be analysed using different methods.

**Discuss **the advantages and disadvantages of analysing a system by interviewing staff rather than using questionnaires.
parts.solution_md:
Analysing a system using interviews instead of questionnaires has several advantages. One benefit is that the interviewer can **clarify any misunderstood questions**, ensuring accurate responses. Additionally, interviews allow for **more detailed answers**, as follow-up questions can be asked based on the interviewee’s responses. Another advantage is that **body language and facial expressions can be observed**, providing extra insight into the interviewee’s opinions.

However, interviews also have disadvantages. **They are not anonymous**, meaning interviewees may feel uncomfortable giving honest answers, especially if they fear repercussions. Additionally, interviews **take longer to complete** than questionnaires, as each person must be spoken to individually. Another drawback is that interviews are** more expensive**, as they require trained interviewers and time off work for staff.

Overall, while interviews provide detailed and flexible responses, questionnaires are quicker, cheaper, and allow for anonymous feedback.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The response includes at least three advantages and three disadvantages, ensuring a balanced discussion.
> 
> - Questions can be explained if misunderstood **[1 mark]**
> - More detailed answers can be given **[1 mark]**
> - Can see body language **[1 mark]**
> - The interview is not anonymous **[1 mark]**
> - Takes far longer to complete than a questionnaire **[1 mark]**
> - More expensive as the interviewer has to be hired and interviewee needs time off **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Five **top tips for answering this 6-mark "discuss" question effectively:
> 
> 1. **Include at least three advantages and three disadvantages**
> 
>   1. A balanced response is necessary to gain full marks.
> 2. **Explain why interviews provide better quality responses**
> 
>   1. Example: Instead of "interviews allow for more detail," write "interviews allow for follow-up questions, leading to more detailed and useful responses."
> 3. **Consider the limitations of interviews**
> 
>   1. Highlight time constraints, lack of anonymity, and costs, which are key disadvantages.
> 4. **Compare interviews with questionnaires directly**
> 
>   1. Example: "Unlike questionnaires, interviews are not anonymous, which may cause employees to withhold honest opinions."
> 5. **Avoid vague statements**
> 
>   1. Instead of "questionnaires are quicker," explain "questionnaires can be distributed to a large number of people and analysed quickly using Optical Mark Recognition (OMR).

**Explain **what is meant by **normal**, **abnormal **and **extreme **test data.
parts.solution_md:
The terms normal, abnormal and extreme when referring to test data mean:

**Normal **

- Data is within the range of acceptability  **[1 mark]**

**Abnormal **

Any **one **of the following:

- Data outside the range of acceptability  **[1 mark]**
- Data that is of an incorrect type  **[1 mark]**

**Extreme **

- Data that is on the boundary/limit of acceptability  **[1 mark]**
